position: both — *a keen eye*, *She wasn't keen on it*
takes: *on* + noun or *-ing* (liking: *keen on jazz*, mostly *not keen on*); *to*-infinitive (wanting to do: *keen to help*)
contrast: *Keen on* + noun or *-ing* means liking something (*I'm not keen on horror movies*); *keen to* + verb means wanting to do it (*She's keen to start*). Never ✗ *keen for doing* or ✗ *keen in*. In American English the 'eager' sense sounds a little British or formal, except in the negative *not too keen on*; Americans more often say *eager to*, *excited about* or *into* (*I'm really into jazz*). The everyday American uses are the 'sharp' and 'strong' ones: *a keen eye*, *a keen sense of smell*, *keen interest*, *keen competition*. *Peachy keen* (great) is old-fashioned, joking slang.

senses.gloss: Of the senses or the mind: sharp and quick to notice or understand.
examples: Dogs have a much *keener* sense of smell than people.
She has a *keen* eye for detail.
He was a *keen* observer of small-town life.

senses.gloss: Of a feeling or interest: strong and deep.
examples: He took a *keen* interest in local politics.
Competition for the job was *keen*.
The company faces *keen* competition from overseas.

senses.gloss: Wanting very much to do something, or liking something very much.
examples: I'm not too *keen* on the idea of camping in January.
The new owners are *keen* to make changes.
She was never very *keen* on sports.

senses.gloss: Of a blade, having a very sharp edge; of wind, cold and biting — literary.
examples: The knife had a *keen* edge.
A *keen* wind blew off the lake.

position: both — *proud parents*, *We're proud of you*
takes: *of* + noun or *-ing* (*proud of you*, *proud of finishing*); *to*-infinitive (*proud to announce*); *that*-clause (*proud that she won*)
contrast: Russian *гордиться* + a noun in the instrumental case becomes *proud of* in English: *I'm proud of my son*, never ✗ *proud with my son*, ✗ *proud for my son* or ✗ *proud by*. *Proud to* + verb is about the honor of doing something now (*proud to be here*); *proud of* + *-ing* is about something done (*proud of winning*). *Proud* can be good (pleased about success, self-respect) or bad (arrogant): context decides, as with *гордый*. The noun is *pride*, and *take pride in* is the verb phrase (*She takes pride in her work*). *Do someone proud* (make them proud) is an adverb idiom.

senses.gloss: Pleased and happy about something you, or someone close to you, did or has.
examples: Your mom and I are so *proud* of you.
I've never been *prouder* of this team.
We're *proud* to announce the opening of our second store.

senses.gloss: Having self-respect and not wanting help or pity from others.
examples: He was too *proud* to ask for money.
They're a *proud* people with a long history.
She's a *proud* woman who hates to complain.

senses.gloss: Thinking that you are better or more important than other people.
examples: He's too *proud* to admit he was wrong.
She was a cold, *proud* woman who looked down on everyone.

senses.gloss: Of a moment, day or thing: causing a feeling of pride.
examples: Graduation was the *proudest* day of my father's life.
It was a *proud* moment for the whole town.
The new stadium is the school's *proudest* achievement.

position: both — *a jealous husband*, *He's jealous of her*
takes: *of* + person or thing (*jealous of her*, *jealous of his success*)
contrast: Russian splits *зависть* and *ревность*; everyday American English uses *jealous* for both: *I'm jealous of your vacation* (завидую) and *He gets jealous when she talks to other guys* (ревнует). *Envious* covers only wanting what someone else has, and is more formal. Russian *завидовать кому-то* takes the dative, but English needs *of*: *jealous of him*, never ✗ *jealous to him* or ✗ *jealous on him*. *I'm so jealous!* is often friendly and light, like *везёт же!*. The verb for the envy sense is *envy* with no preposition (*I envy you*); there is no verb *to jealous*.

senses.gloss: Unhappy because someone has something you want.
examples: Everyone at work is *jealous* of her new office.
I'm so *jealous* — I've always wanted to go to Hawaii.
He was *jealous* of his brother's success.

senses.gloss: Afraid that someone you love is attracted to, or loves, someone else.
examples: Her boyfriend gets *jealous* when she goes out without him.
He was the *most jealous* husband I've ever met.
The dog gets *jealous* whenever we hold the baby.

senses.gloss: Protecting carefully something you have or value.
examples: The family is *jealous* of its privacy.
She kept a *jealous* watch over her little brother.

position: both — *a capable manager*, *She's capable of more*
takes: *of* + noun or *-ing* (*capable of anything*, *capable of running a marathon*), never a *to*-infinitive
contrast: *Capable of* + *-ing*, never ✗ *capable to do*: *She's capable of doing it*, but *She's able to do it*. The two words take different patterns, and learners mix them. Russian *способный ученик* (talented, quick) is usually *a bright student* or *a gifted student*; *a capable student* means competent and reliable, not especially gifted. *Способен на всё* is *capable of anything*, often with a hint that the person might do something bad.

senses.gloss: Having the ability, power or capacity to do something.
examples: The truck is *capable* of pulling a small boat.
You're *capable* of much better work than this.
The new stadium is *capable* of holding 60,000 fans.

senses.gloss: Able to do things well; competent and skilled.
examples: Don't worry — the kids are in very *capable* hands.
She's the *most capable* manager we've ever had.
He seemed *capable* and calm in a crisis.

senses.gloss: Willing or likely to do something bad or surprising.
examples: I didn't think he was *capable* of lying to me.
When she's angry, she's *capable* of anything.

position: both — *a similar problem*, *The two houses are similar*
takes: *to* + noun (*similar to mine*); *in* + the feature that is alike (*similar in size*)
contrast: *Similar to*, never ✗ *similar with*, ✗ *similar as* or ✗ *similar on*. Russian *похож на* suggests *on*, but English uses *to*. For the feature, use *in*: *similar in color*, not ✗ *similar by color*. *Similar* means alike, not identical: for identical use *the same as* (*My phone is the same as yours*) or *identical to*. For people's faces, *look like* is more natural: *She looks like her mother* rather than *She is similar to her mother*. The comparative is *more similar*, never ✗ *similarer*.

senses.gloss: Almost the same as someone or something, but not exactly.
examples: Your car is very *similar* to mine.
The two sisters are *similar* in size, so they share clothes.
The new version is *more similar* to the original than I expected.

senses.gloss: In geometry: having the same shape but not the same size.
examples: The two triangles are *similar* because their angles are equal.
Show that the triangles are *similar*.

position: both — *a different color*, *Her plan is different*
takes: *from* + noun (standard); *than* + noun or clause (common American, best before a clause); *to* is British
contrast: *Different from* is always correct in American English (*Her account is different from his*). *Different than* is common and natural before a clause (*It was different than I expected*); before a noun some editors still prefer *from*. *Different to* is British. Russian *другой* has three English matches: *different* (not the same: *a different answer*), *another* (one more or a replacement, singular: *another cup*), and *other* (*the other side*). Before a plural noun, *different* often means *разные* (*different colors*). The adverb is *differently*: *She thinks differently*, not *She thinks different* in careful English. Grade it with *very*, *completely* or *a little*; *no different* means exactly the same (*Today was no different*).

senses.gloss: Not the same as someone or something else.
examples: My brother is completely *different* from me.
The job turned out to be *different* than I expected.
Life in the city couldn't be *more different* from life on the farm.

senses.gloss: Before a plural noun: separate and of several kinds.
examples: The shirt comes in five *different* colors.
I've called three *different* times and nobody answers.
People have *different* reasons for moving here.

senses.gloss: Not the one already mentioned or usual; another.
examples: Can I try a *different* size?
She moved to a *different* school in the fall.
Let's talk about something *different*.

senses.gloss: Unusual or new, sometimes as a polite way to say you do not like something.
examples: Well, the color is certainly *different*.
I wanted something *different* for my birthday this year.

position: both — *a typical day*, *That's typical of him*
takes: *of* + person or group (*typical of him*); *for* + place, time or group, common in American English (*typical for July*); *of* + person + *to*-infinitive (*It's typical of her to be late*)
contrast: For behavior, *It's typical of him to* + verb is the standard pattern; *typical for him* is common in speech but less careful. For places and times, American English uses both: *typical of* and *typical for this time of year*. Never ✗ *typical to him*. *Typical!* on its own is a complaint: something annoying has happened again, as expected — *как всегда!*. Russian *обычный* matches *typical* only before a noun (*on a typical day* — в обычный день); after a verb use *normal* or *usual* (*That's normal*).

senses.gloss: Having the usual qualities of a particular kind of person, thing or group.
examples: It was a *typical* American breakfast: eggs, bacon and pancakes.
This is *typical* of houses built in the 1950s.
Heavy rain is *typical* for this time of year.

senses.gloss: Normal and average; happening in the usual way.
examples: On a *typical* day, I get to the office at eight.
The *most typical* customer is a woman in her thirties.
A *typical* family here has two cars.

senses.gloss: Behaving in the annoying way you expect of someone or something.
examples: It's *typical* of him to leave the dishes for me.
The bus is late again. *Typical*!
That's so *typical* of this company.

position: both — *related issues*, *The two problems are related*
comparison: more/most — usually with *closely*: *more closely related*, *most closely related*
takes: *to* + noun (connection or family: *related to the case*, *related to me*)
contrast: *Related to*, never ✗ *related with*: Russian *связан с* pulls toward *with*, but English uses *to*. *Are you two related?* asks whether people are family; the noun for the person is *a relative*, not *a related*. *Relative* as an adjective means compared with something else (*relative safety*) and is a different word. In compounds, *-related* means caused by or connected with: *a work-related injury*, *alcohol-related crashes*.

senses.gloss: Connected with something, often by cause.
examples: Police think the two robberies are *related*.
She asked a few questions *related* to the budget.
He takes a lot of sick days for stress-*related* health problems.

senses.gloss: In the same family, by birth or marriage.
examples: Are you *related* to the Johnsons down the street?
We have the same last name, but we're not *related*.
She's *related* to me by marriage.

senses.gloss: Of languages, animals or plants: coming from the same origin.
examples: Russian and Polish are closely *related* languages.
Humans are *more closely related* to chimps than to gorillas.

position: both — *used to* after a verb (*I'm used to it*); *used* meaning secondhand before a noun (*a used car*)
comparison: more/most — in the *accustomed* sense: *more used to*, *so used to*; not gradable in the *secondhand* sense
takes: *to* + noun or *-ing* after *be*, *get* or *become* (*used to the noise*, *used to working nights*)
contrast: Two different things are spelled *used to*. The adjective, after *be* or *get*, means accustomed and needs a noun or *-ing*: *I'm used to getting up early*, never ✗ *I'm used to get up early*. The habit-in-the-past form has no *be* and takes a bare verb: *I used to get up early* (раньше вставал рано, а теперь нет). *Be used to* is the state (привык); *get used to* is the process (привыкнуть): *You'll get used to it*. In *used to* both are said /juːst/, with the *s* of *loose*; *a used car* has /juːzd/, with a *z*. For a verb meaning 'employed', *used* is a passive verb, not this adjective: *This room is used for storage*.

senses.gloss: Familiar with something, so that it no longer seems strange or difficult.
examples: I'm not *used* to this heat yet.
You'll get *used* to working nights after a week or two.
After a year in Chicago, she's *more used* to the cold.

senses.gloss: Owned by someone else before; not new.
examples: We bought a *used* car for our daughter.
The store sells *used* books and records.

senses.gloss: Already used once, so not clean or not able to be used again.
examples: Put the *used* towels in the basket.
Throw *used* needles into the red container.

position: both — *accustomed to* after a verb (*She's accustomed to it*); before a noun it means usual (*his accustomed seat*)
takes: *to* + noun or *-ing* after *be*, *get*, *become* or *grow* (*accustomed to the noise*, *accustomed to working late*)
contrast: The *to* is a preposition, so a verb after it takes *-ing*: *accustomed to driving*, not ✗ *accustomed to drive* (that older pattern survives only in very formal writing). *Accustomed to* means the same as *used to* but is more formal; in conversation Americans say *I'm used to it*. *Be accustomed* is the state; *get*, *become* or *grow accustomed* is the change. Before a noun, *accustomed* means usual and is literary: *in her accustomed place*.

senses.gloss: Familiar with something because you have experienced it often.
examples: She's *accustomed* to working long hours.
My eyes slowly grew *accustomed* to the dark.
The kids became *more accustomed* to the new school by spring.

senses.gloss: Before a noun: usual or habitual — formal.
examples: He sat in his *accustomed* seat by the window.
She answered with her *accustomed* calm.

position: both — *a familiar face*, *The name sounds familiar*
takes: *with* + thing (the person knows it: *familiar with the software*); *to* + person (it is known to them: *familiar to most Americans*)
contrast: The preposition swaps the subject. *I'm familiar with the song* means I know it; *The song is familiar to me* means the same thing from the other side. Never ✗ *I'm familiar to the song*. Russian *знаком с* matches *familiar with* for things, but for people you have met, English prefers *know* or *have met*: *I know him*, not *I'm familiar with him*, which sounds like you only know about him. *Фамильярный* is only one sense (too informal), and the Russian noun *знакомый* (a person you know) is *an acquaintance*, not *a familiar*.

senses.gloss: Known to you, or easy to recognize because you have seen or heard it before.
examples: It was nice to see a *familiar* face at the party.
Your name sounds *familiar* — have we met?
The story will be *familiar* to anyone who grew up in a small town.

senses.gloss: Knowing something well.
examples: Are you *familiar* with this software?
I'm not very *familiar* with the area.
After a month, she was *more familiar* with the rules.

senses.gloss: Friendly and informal, sometimes too informal with someone you do not know well.
examples: He was a little too *familiar* with the waitress.
The two men were on *familiar* terms after years of working together.

position: both — *a famous singer*, *She became famous*
takes: *for* + what makes it known (*famous for its pizza*); *as* + role (*famous as a singer*)
contrast: *Famous for*, never ✗ *famous by*, ✗ *famous with* or ✗ *famous of*: *The city is famous for its jazz* (славится джазом). *Famous as* names the role: *famous as an actor*. For fame for something bad, use *notorious* or *infamous*; *infamous* is not the opposite of *famous* but its dark side, and it is stressed IN-fuh-muhs. Russian *известный* is often just *well-known* (*a well-known doctor in town*); *famous* is stronger, known to very many people.

senses.gloss: Known about by very many people.
examples: New Orleans is *famous* for its food and music.
He was *famous* as a boxer before he went into politics.
The Grand Canyon is one of the *most famous* sights in America.

position: both — *an anxious mother*, *She was anxious about it*
takes: *about* + noun or *-ing* (worry: *anxious about the test*); *for* + person (worry for them: *anxious for his safety*) or + thing (wanting it: *anxious for news*); *to*-infinitive (eager: *anxious to leave*); *that*-clause
contrast: The preposition changes the meaning. *Anxious about* is worry (*anxious about money*). *Anxious to* + verb and *anxious for* + thing usually mean eager, often with a little impatience (*anxious to get home*, *anxious for news*). Some American usage guides object to *anxious* for 'eager' and prefer *eager*, but it is very common. *Anxious* is stronger and more lasting than *nervous*: you are *nervous* before a speech, *anxious* about your health.

senses.gloss: Worried and nervous about something that might happen.
examples: She's *anxious* about her job interview tomorrow.
The longer we waited, the *more anxious* I got.
Parents are *anxious* for the safety of their kids.

senses.gloss: Of a time or a look: full of worry, or causing it.
examples: There were a few *anxious* moments before the plane landed.
After an *anxious* wait, the doctor came out.

senses.gloss: Wanting very much to do or have something, often impatiently.
examples: We're *anxious* to get home before dark.
The company is *anxious* for a quick deal.
He was *anxious* that nobody should find out.

position: both — *eager fans*, *She was eager to help*
takes: *to*-infinitive (*eager to help*); *for* + noun (*eager for news*)
contrast: *Eager to* + verb, never ✗ *eager of doing* or ✗ *eager in doing*; for a noun use *for*: *eager for success*. *Eager* is all positive expectation; *anxious to* adds worry or impatience. *Eager to please* describes someone who tries hard to make others happy. *An eager beaver* is an informal American name for a very enthusiastic, hard-working person.

senses.gloss: Wanting very much to do or have something.
examples: The kids were *eager* to open their presents.
Fans are *eager* for news about the next season.
Nobody was *more eager* to start than the new guy.

senses.gloss: Full of interest and enthusiasm.
examples: The teacher looked out at a room full of *eager* faces.
He's an *eager* student who always asks questions.
The new puppy is friendly and *eager* to please.

position: both — *suitable clothes*, *The room is suitable*
takes: *for* + person, purpose or *-ing* (*suitable for kids*, *suitable for camping*); *as* + role (*suitable as a gift*)
contrast: *Suitable for*, never ✗ *suitable to* + person or ✗ *suitable with*: *suitable for children*. *Suitable* is somewhat formal; in speech Americans often say *good for*, *right for* or *appropriate for*. Russian *подходить* is a verb, and English has verbs too: *suit* and *fit* (*The job suits her*, *The dress fits*). *Suitable* is about being right for a purpose, not about size: a jacket that is the right size *fits*; a jacket that is right for a wedding is *suitable*.

senses.gloss: Right or appropriate for a particular person, purpose or occasion.
examples: This movie isn't *suitable* for young children.
We're still looking for a *suitable* place for the party.
Jeans would be *more suitable* for a hike than that skirt.

position: both — *sensitive skin*, *She's sensitive about her age*
takes: *to* + noun (reacting to, or aware of: *sensitive to light*, *sensitive to her needs*); *about* + noun (easily upset about: *sensitive about his weight*)
contrast: *Sensitive to* is reacting or being aware (*sensitive to criticism*, *sensitive to the cold*); *sensitive about* is getting upset about a personal matter (*sensitive about her accent*). *Sensitive* is a false friend of *sensible*, which means *разумный*: *a sensible decision* (разумное решение), *a sensitive person* (чуткий или обидчивый человек). Russian *чувствительный* is close, but *чуткий* (caring) is often *thoughtful* or *understanding* in speech.

senses.gloss: Reacting quickly or strongly to something physical, such as light, cold or a substance.
examples: Use a mild soap if you have *sensitive* skin.
My eyes are very *sensitive* to light.
Babies are *more sensitive* to heat than adults.

senses.gloss: Understanding other people's feelings and needs.
examples: He's a kind, *sensitive* guy.
Doctors need to be *sensitive* to their patients' fears.

senses.gloss: Easily hurt or upset by what people say or do.
examples: She's very *sensitive* about her weight, so don't mention it.
Don't be so *sensitive* — I was only joking.
Teenagers can be *sensitive* to criticism.

senses.gloss: Needing to be handled carefully because it could upset people or is secret.
examples: Money is a *sensitive* subject in our family.
The files contain *sensitive* information.

senses.gloss: Of a machine or instrument: able to measure or detect very small changes.
examples: The microphone is *sensitive* enough to pick up a whisper.
The test is the *most sensitive* one available.

position: both — *dependent children*, *She's dependent on her parents*
takes: *on* or formal *upon* + noun or *-ing* (*dependent on oil*, *dependent on getting a loan*)
contrast: Russian *зависеть от* pulls toward ✗ *dependent from*, but English says *dependent on*: *The price is dependent on the season*. The verb works the same way: *It depends on the weather*. In American English the noun for a person you support is also spelled *dependent* (*You can claim two dependents on your taxes*); British English spells that noun *dependant*.

senses.gloss: Needing someone or something for support, money or help.
examples: At 25, he's still *dependent* on his parents.
The town is heavily *dependent* on tourism.
The country has become *more dependent* on imported oil.

senses.gloss: Needing a drug or alcohol regularly and unable to stop.
examples: She became *dependent* on painkillers after the surgery.
The clinic helps people who are alcohol-*dependent*.

senses.gloss: Decided by or changing with something else.
examples: Your raise is *dependent* on your performance.
Whether we go is *dependent* on the weather.

senses.gloss: In grammar: of a clause, not able to stand alone as a sentence.
examples: In *When I got home, I ate*, the first clause is *dependent*.
A *dependent* clause usually starts with a word like *because* or *if*.

position: both — *an independent country*, *She's very independent*
takes: *of* + noun (standard: *independent of her parents*); *from* + noun, common for countries and organizations (*independent from Britain*)
contrast: *Dependent on* but *independent of* (or *from*): the preposition changes with the prefix, so ✗ *independent on* is wrong. *Independent of* also means 'without regard to': *Prices rose independent of demand*. *An independent* is also a noun in American politics: a voter or candidate who is not a Democrat or a Republican. Russian *самостоятельный* about a person or child is *independent*, not *self-standing*.

senses.gloss: Of a person: able to take care of yourself and make your own decisions.
examples: My grandmother is 90 and still very *independent*.
Kids become *more independent* as they get older.
She got a job so she could be *independent* of her parents.

senses.gloss: Of a country or organization: not controlled or owned by another.
examples: The country became *independent* in 1991.
He works for a small *independent* bookstore.
The review was done by an *independent* expert.

senses.gloss: Not connected with or affected by something else.
examples: Two *independent* studies found the same result.
The two systems are completely *independent* of each other.

senses.gloss: Not belonging to a political party.
examples: She's running for Senate as an *independent* candidate.
*Independent* voters will decide this election.

senses.gloss: In grammar: of a clause, able to stand alone as a sentence.
examples: An *independent* clause has a subject and a verb and makes sense alone.
Join two *independent* clauses with a comma and *and*.

position: both — mostly after a verb (*We're opposed to the plan*); before a noun only in the *opposite* sense (*two opposed views*)
takes: *to* + noun or *-ing* (*opposed to the plan*, *opposed to raising taxes*)
contrast: The *to* is a preposition, so a verb after it takes *-ing*: *opposed to raising taxes*, never ✗ *opposed to raise taxes*. The verb *oppose* takes a direct object with no *to*: *They oppose the plan*, not ✗ *They oppose to the plan*. *As opposed to* is a fixed phrase meaning 'rather than, in contrast with' (*в отличие от*): *real leather as opposed to plastic*. Before a noun meaning 'on the other side', use *opposing*: *the opposing team*.

senses.gloss: Disagreeing strongly with a plan, idea or action and wanting to stop it.
examples: Most people in town are *opposed* to the new highway.
I'm not *opposed* to working weekends if the pay is good.
The senator is *more opposed* to the bill than ever.

senses.gloss: Completely different from each other.
examples: The two parties hold diametrically *opposed* views.
Their goals are directly *opposed*.

position: both — *a crazy idea*, *You're crazy*
takes: *about* + person or thing (loving it: *crazy about her*, *crazy about baseball*); *to*-infinitive (foolish: *crazy to go*); *with* + feeling (*crazy with worry*)
contrast: *Crazy about* means loving someone or something (*I'm crazy about you*, *без ума от тебя*); *crazy at* is wrong. *Drive someone crazy* means annoy them very much; *go crazy* can mean get angry, lose control, or get very excited (*The crowd went crazy*). *Like crazy* is an adverb phrase meaning very much or very fast (*We worked like crazy*). Using *crazy* about someone with a mental illness is offensive. As slang, *crazy* before another adjective is an adverb: *crazy good*.

senses.gloss: Very foolish or not sensible.
examples: You're *crazy* to drive in this snow.
That's the *craziest* idea I've ever heard.
It sounds *crazy*, but it just might work.

senses.gloss: Very busy, wild or without order.
examples: It's been a *crazy* week at work.
Traffic downtown was *crazy* this morning.
When the band came out, the crowd went *crazy*.

senses.gloss: Very angry or annoyed.
examples: That noise is driving me *crazy*.
My dad will go *crazy* when he sees the car.

senses.gloss: Liking someone or something very much.
examples: She's *crazy* about her new boyfriend.
My son is *crazy* about dinosaurs.
I'm not *crazy* about the color, but it's OK.

senses.gloss: Mentally ill — informal and often offensive.
examples: In the movie, a *crazy* man lives alone in the woods.
People used to think she was *crazy*, but she was just lonely.

position: both — *a mad dog*, *Are you mad at me?*
takes: *at* + person (angry: *mad at me*); *about* + thing (angry about it, or loving it: *mad about the delay*, *mad about jazz*); *with* + feeling (*mad with grief*)
contrast: In everyday American English *mad* usually means angry: *Are you mad at me?* (ты на меня злишься?). In British English it usually means crazy. So *My mom is mad* in the US means she is angry, not insane. Use *mad at* for a person and *mad about* for a situation: *mad at her boss*, *mad about the parking ticket*. *Mad about* can also mean loving something, like *crazy about*; context decides. *Like mad* is an adverb phrase (*run like mad*), and *madly in love* uses the adverb.

senses.gloss: Angry — the usual American meaning.
examples: Are you still *mad* at me about last night?
He got *mad* when I told him about the dent.
I've never seen her *madder* than when they canceled her flight.

senses.gloss: Very foolish or wild; not sensible.
examples: It was a *mad* idea to drive all night.
There was a *mad* rush for the doors when the store opened.

senses.gloss: Mentally ill — old-fashioned or literary in American English.
examples: In the story, a *mad* scientist builds a monster.
She was nearly *mad* with grief.

senses.gloss: Liking something or someone very much.
examples: He's *mad* about old cars.
The whole town went *mad* for the new pizza place.

senses.gloss: Of an animal: having rabies.
examples: Stay away from that dog — it might be *mad*.
Farmers once feared *mad* foxes.

senses.gloss: Slang: a lot of, or very great.
examples: That kid has *mad* skills on the court.
*Mad* respect to everyone who came out tonight.

position: both — after a verb (*She's upset*); before a noun (*an upset customer*, *an upset stomach*), where the stress often moves to UHP-set
takes: *about* + thing (*upset about the news*); *with* + person (*upset with me*); *at* + thing or person; *by* + cause; *that*-clause; *to*-infinitive (*upset to hear it*)
contrast: *Upset about* a thing, *upset with* a person: *She's upset about the grade* but *She's upset with her teacher*. *Upset* is milder than *angry*: it mixes sadness, worry and annoyance, close to *расстроен* or *обижен*. The verb is *upset*, *upset*, *upset*, never ✗ *upsetted*. *Upsetting* describes what causes the feeling (*upsetting news*). The noun *an upset* (UHP-set) is a surprise defeat in sports (*a big upset in the playoffs*).

senses.gloss: Unhappy, worried or disappointed because something bad happened.
examples: She was really *upset* about losing her phone.
Don't get *upset* — it's just a game.
The kids were *more upset* than we expected when the dog died.

senses.gloss: Annoyed and hurt by what someone did.
examples: Are you *upset* with me for leaving early?
My boss was *upset* that nobody called him.

senses.gloss: Of the stomach: slightly sick.
examples: I have an *upset* stomach, so I'll skip dinner.
Spicy food can leave you with an *upset* stomach.

position: both — *a nervous smile*, *I'm nervous*; in the *nerves* sense before a noun only (*the nervous system*)
takes: *about* + noun or *-ing* (*nervous about the test*, *nervous about flying*); *around* + person (*nervous around dogs*)
contrast: *Nervous* in English means worried and a little afraid: *I'm nervous about my interview* is *я волнуюсь перед собеседованием*. Russian *нервный* about someone's temper (irritable, quick to anger) is usually *on edge*, *irritable*, *jumpy* or *short-tempered*, not *nervous*. *Nervous about*, not ✗ *nervous for* in careful English (though *nervous for someone* is heard for worry on another's behalf). *A nervous breakdown* is a serious mental collapse, not just being upset.

senses.gloss: Worried and a little afraid about something that is going to happen.
examples: I always get *nervous* before I speak in public.
She's *nervous* about driving on the highway.
The closer the date got, the *more nervous* he was.

senses.gloss: Easily worried or frightened by nature.
examples: He's a *nervous* flyer.
Our cat is *nervous* around strangers.
She gave a *nervous* laugh.

senses.gloss: Before a noun: of the nerves in the body.
examples: The brain is part of the central *nervous* system.
He had a *nervous* breakdown after the divorce.

position: both — *a sick child*, *I feel sick*
takes: *with* + illness or feeling (*sick with the flu*, *sick with worry*); *from* + cause (*sick from the shrimp*); *of* + noun or *-ing* (fed up: *sick of waiting*); *to* + *my stomach* (nausea); *about* + thing (upset or guilty: *I feel sick about it*)
contrast: In American English *sick* is the everyday word for ill: *I'm sick*, *She called in sick*. *Ill* sounds more formal. In British English *be sick* usually means vomit; Americans say *throw up* or *I'm going to be sick*. *Sick with* names the illness (*sick with a cold*) and *sick from* names the cause (*sick from the shrimp*); ✗ *sick by* is wrong. *Sick of* means fed up (*надоело*): *I'm sick of this weather*, often *sick and tired of*. *Sick leave* and *a sick day* are nouns used as modifiers.

senses.gloss: Not healthy; having an illness.
examples: I can't come in today — I'm *sick*.
She was *sick* with the flu all last week.
He got *sicker* and had to go to the hospital.

senses.gloss: Feeling that you are going to vomit.
examples: The boat ride made me feel *sick*.
I was *sick* to my stomach all night.

senses.gloss: Tired of something and annoyed by it.
examples: I'm *sick* of eating the same thing every day.
We're all *sick* and tired of your excuses.

senses.gloss: Very upset, disgusted or guilty about something.
examples: It makes me *sick* to see how they treat those animals.
I felt *sick* about lying to her.

senses.gloss: Cruel or strange in a way that shocks or disgusts people.
examples: That's a *sick* joke, and it isn't funny.
Whoever did this has a *sick* mind.

senses.gloss: Slang: excellent, very impressive.
examples: Did you see that trick? That was *sick*!
He has the *sickest* car in the neighborhood.

position: both — *a guilty look*, *I feel guilty*
takes: *about* + noun or *-ing* (the feeling: *guilty about lying*); *for* + noun or *-ing* (*guilty for leaving*); *of* + crime or *-ing* (legal: *guilty of fraud*); *to* + charge after *plead* (*pleaded guilty to theft*)
contrast: The feeling takes *about* or *for* (*I feel guilty about forgetting her birthday*); the legal fact takes *of* (*He was found guilty of theft*), never ✗ *guilty in theft* even though Russian says *виновен в*. In everyday speech Russian *я виноват* is usually *It's my fault* or *I'm sorry*, not *I'm guilty*, which sounds like a courtroom. *Plead guilty* and *plead not guilty* are the court phrases. *A guilty pleasure* is something you enjoy but are a little embarrassed about.

senses.gloss: Feeling bad because you did something wrong or did not do something you should have.
examples: I feel *guilty* about not calling my mom more often.
She felt *guiltier* every time he thanked her.
Don't feel *guilty* for taking a day off.

senses.gloss: Having done a crime or a wrong thing, especially as decided by a court.
examples: The jury found him *guilty* of murder.
She pleaded *guilty* to drunk driving.
We were all *guilty* of ignoring the problem.

senses.gloss: Showing or causing a feeling of guilt.
examples: The dog gave me a *guilty* look.
Reality TV is my *guilty* pleasure.
He has a *guilty* conscience.

position: both — *innocent victims*, *He's innocent*
takes: *of* + crime (legal: *innocent of the charges*)
contrast: *Innocent of* a crime, never ✗ *innocent in*: Russian *невиновен в* pulls toward *in*. English uses one word where Russian has two: *невиновный* (not guilty) and *невинный* (naive, pure) are both *innocent*. In American courts a jury finds someone *not guilty*, not *innocent*; *innocent until proven guilty* is the principle. *An innocent question* is a harmless one, not a naive one.

senses.gloss: Not guilty of a crime.
examples: He spent ten years in prison, but he was *innocent*.
She was declared *innocent* of all charges.
Everyone is *innocent* until proven guilty.

senses.gloss: Harmed by something without having done anything to cause it.
senses.ru: ни в чём не повинный; мирный (о жертвах)
examples: Two *innocent* bystanders were hurt in the shooting.
The war killed thousands of *innocent* people.

senses.gloss: Knowing little about the bad things in life; naive.
examples: She was just an *innocent* kid from a small town.
Those were *more innocent* times.

senses.gloss: Not meant to cause harm or offense.
examples: It was an *innocent* question — I didn't mean to upset you.
It was an *innocent* mistake.

position: both — mostly after a verb (*I'm grateful*); before a noun formal (*a grateful nation*)
takes: *to* + person (*grateful to my teachers*); *for* + thing or *-ing* (*grateful for your help*); *that*-clause; *to*-infinitive (*grateful to be here*)
contrast: The full pattern is *grateful to* a person *for* a thing, like Russian *благодарен кому-то за что-то*: *I'm grateful to you for your help*. Never ✗ *grateful for you* when you mean the person helped (*grateful for you* means glad you exist). *I'd be grateful if you could...* is a polite written request. The spelling is *grateful*, not ✗ *greatful*: the word is not related to *great*. *Grateful* is gratitude to someone; *thankful* is more often relief that something happened.

senses.gloss: Feeling or showing thanks to someone for something.
examples: I'm really *grateful* to you for helping us move.
We're *grateful* for everything the nurses did.
I couldn't be *more grateful* that you came.

position: both — mostly after a verb (*We're thankful*); before a noun less often (*a thankful heart*)
takes: *for* + thing (*thankful for my family*); *that*-clause (*thankful that nobody was hurt*); *to*-infinitive (*thankful to be alive*); *to* + person, less often than with *grateful*
contrast: *Thankful* is usually about relief or luck, not about a person: *I'm thankful nobody was hurt* (слава богу, никто не пострадал). For thanks to a specific person, *grateful to* is more natural: *I'm grateful to you*. At Thanksgiving Americans say what they are *thankful for* (*I'm thankful for my health*). *Thankfully* means 'luckily': *Thankfully, it didn't rain*.

senses.gloss: Feeling grateful for the good things you have.
examples: This Thanksgiving, I'm *thankful* for my family and friends.
I've never been *more thankful* for a warm bed.
Be *thankful* for what you have.

senses.gloss: Glad and relieved that something happened or did not happen.
examples: We're just *thankful* that nobody was hurt.
I was *thankful* to be home after that trip.

position: both — *a kind woman*, *She was kind to me*
takes: *to* + person or animal (*kind to kids*); *of* + person + *to*-infinitive (*kind of you to come*); *enough to* (*kind enough to help*)
contrast: *Kind to* describes how someone treats others (*She's kind to everyone*); *It's kind of you to* + verb thanks someone for a particular act (*It's so kind of you to call*). Don't confuse this with the noun *kind* (sort, type: *What kind of music?*) or with *kind of* as an informal adverb meaning 'a little' (*I'm kind of tired*). Russian *добрый* about a person is usually *kind* or *nice*, not *good*; *Добрый день* is just *Good afternoon*. *Kind regards* ends a polite email.

senses.gloss: Caring about others and treating them in a friendly, generous way.
examples: Our neighbors have always been *kind* to us.
She's one of the *kindest* people I know.
He said some *kind* words about my dad at the funeral.

senses.gloss: Used politely to thank someone or to ask for something.
examples: It was very *kind* of you to drive me home.
Would you be *kind* enough to close the window?

senses.gloss: Gentle and not harmful.
examples: This shampoo is *kind* to sensitive skin.
The years have been *kind* to her — she looks great.

position: both — *a polite answer*, *He's always polite*
takes: *to* + person (*polite to guests*); *of* + person + *to*-infinitive (*polite of you to ask*); *to*-infinitive (*It's polite to call first*)
contrast: *Polite to* a person, not ✗ *polite with*: *Be polite to your grandmother*. *More polite* and *most polite* are far more common in American English than *politer* and *politest*. *Polite* can be cool rather than warm: *polite applause* is thin clapping, *polite conversation* is small talk. For *вежливый, но холодный* use *polite but distant*.

senses.gloss: Having good manners and respect for other people.
examples: The kids were very *polite* to our guests.
It's *polite* to ask before you take the last piece.
Could you try to be a little *more polite*?

senses.gloss: Correct and socially proper, but not warm or sincere.
examples: The speech got only *polite* applause.
We made *polite* conversation until the food came.

senses.gloss: Of a group or setting: respectable and having refined manners.
examples: That's not a word you use in *polite* company.
Politics wasn't discussed in *polite* society.

position: both — *a rude waiter*, *He was rude to me*
takes: *to* + person (*rude to the waiter*); *of* + person + *to*-infinitive (*rude of him to leave*); *to*-infinitive (*It's rude to stare*); *about* + thing (*rude about her cooking*)
contrast: *Rude to* a person, never ✗ *rude with*. English *rude* covers only bad manners and vulgarity; Russian *грубый* is much wider. *Грубая ткань* is *coarse fabric*, *грубая ошибка* is *a serious* or *glaring mistake*, *грубая сила* is *brute force*, and *грубая оценка* is *a rough estimate*. *A rude awakening* is a sudden unpleasant discovery, not a rough wake-up call.

senses.gloss: Not polite; showing no respect for other people.
examples: The woman at the counter was really *rude* to me.
It's *rude* to check your phone during dinner.
He was the *rudest* customer I've ever had.

senses.gloss: Offensive and connected with sex or the body.
examples: The driver made a *rude* gesture and sped off.
The kids giggled at a *rude* word in the song.

senses.gloss: Sudden, unexpected and unpleasant.
examples: If he thinks the job will be easy, he's in for a *rude* awakening.
The cold weather came as a *rude* shock.

senses.gloss: Simple and roughly made — literary.
examples: The settlers lived in *rude* wooden huts.
They built a *rude* shelter from branches.

position: both — *a nice day*, *You look nice*
takes: *to* + person (behavior: *nice to me*); *of* + person + *to*-infinitive (*nice of you to call*); *to*-infinitive (*nice to meet you*); *about* + thing (kind and understanding: *nice about it*); *that*-clause
contrast: *Nice to* describes how someone treats people (*She's nice to everyone*); *nice of you to* + verb thanks someone for a particular act (*That's nice of you to offer*). *Nice to meet you* is said when you meet; *Nice meeting you* or *Nice talking to you* when you leave. *Nice and* + adjective means pleasantly so: *nice and warm* (тепло и уютно). *Nice* is mild praise; for strong praise use *great* or *wonderful*. Said sarcastically, *Nice!* or *Nice going!* means the opposite (*ну молодец!*).

senses.gloss: Pleasant, enjoyable or attractive.
examples: We had *nice* weather the whole week.
You look *nice* in that dress.
This hotel is much *nicer* than the last one.

senses.gloss: Kind and friendly.
examples: Our new neighbors are really *nice*.
Be *nice* to your little sister.
It was *nice* of you to remember my birthday.

senses.gloss: Done well or with skill — used as praise.
examples: *Nice* shot!
That's a *nice* piece of work.

senses.gloss: Used ironically about something bad.
examples: *Nice* going — you just locked the keys in the car.
Well, this is a *nice* mess you've gotten us into.

senses.gloss: Respectable and well-behaved.
examples: She's a *nice* girl from a *nice* family.
They live in a *nice* neighborhood.

senses.gloss: Of a difference or point: small and subtle — formal.
examples: That's a rather *nice* distinction.
The case turns on a *nice* point of law.

position: both — *a mean thing to say*, *Don't be mean*
takes: *to* + person (*mean to his sister*); *of* + person + *to*-infinitive (*mean of you to say that*); *about* + thing
contrast: In American English *mean* is the everyday word for unkind (*Stop being mean to your brother* — перестань обижать брата). In British English it more often means stingy; Americans say *cheap* for that. *Mean to* a person, not ✗ *mean with*. Don't confuse the adjective with the verb *mean* (значить, иметь в виду: *What do you mean?*), the noun *the mean* (среднее) or *means* (средства). As slang, *mean* can be praise: *She plays a mean guitar* (классно играет). *No mean feat* means a real achievement.

senses.gloss: Unkind or nasty to other people.
examples: The other kids were *mean* to him at school.
That was a really *mean* thing to say.
She's the *meanest* boss I've ever had.

senses.gloss: Of an animal or person: aggressive and likely to attack.
examples: Watch out for their dog — he's *mean*.
He looked like a big, *mean* guy, but he was gentle.

senses.gloss: Not willing to spend or share money — mostly British; Americans say *cheap*.
examples: He's too *mean* to buy anyone a drink.
Don't be so *mean* with the tip.

senses.gloss: Informal: very good or skillful.
examples: My uncle makes a *mean* barbecue.
She plays a *mean* game of pool.

senses.gloss: no mean: very good or difficult — in *no mean feat*, *no mean achievement*.
examples: Raising four kids alone is no *mean* feat.
She's no *mean* cook herself.

senses.gloss: Poor, dirty or dangerous — literary.
examples: He grew up on the *mean* streets of the South Side.
They lived in a *mean* little apartment.

senses.gloss: Before a noun: average, in math and science.
examples: The *mean* annual temperature here is 55 degrees.
Calculate the *mean* score for each group.

position: both — *a cruel joke*, *He was cruel to her*
takes: *to* + person or animal (*cruel to animals*)
contrast: *Cruel to*, not ✗ *cruel with*; *cruel toward* is possible but more formal. American spelling keeps one *l*: *crueler*, *cruelest*; *crueller* and *cruellest* are British. *Cruel* is much stronger than *mean*: *mean* is unkind, *cruel* is causing real pain on purpose. *Cruel and unusual punishment* is a phrase from the US Constitution.

senses.gloss: Wanting to cause pain or suffering, or not caring about it.
examples: He was arrested for being *cruel* to animals.
Kids can be *cruel* to anyone who is different.
It was the *cruelest* thing anyone had ever said to her.

senses.gloss: Of events or conditions: causing great suffering.
examples: By a *cruel* twist of fate, he died the day before his wedding.
It was a long, *cruel* winter.

position: both — *an allergic reaction*, *I'm allergic to cats*
takes: *to* + noun (*allergic to peanuts*)
contrast: Russian *аллергия на* pulls toward ✗ *allergic on*, but English uses *to* for both the adjective and the noun: *I'm allergic to cats*, *an allergy to cats*. *I have an allergy* and *I'm allergic* are both natural; ✗ *I have allergic* is wrong. *Allergic* is pronounced uh-LUR-jik, with the stress on the second syllable, unlike *allergy* (AL-ur-jee).

senses.gloss: Having a bad physical reaction to something you eat, touch or breathe.
examples: My son is *allergic* to peanuts.
Are you *allergic* to any medications?
She's *more allergic* to cats than to dogs.

senses.gloss: Before a noun: caused by an allergy.
examples: He had an *allergic* reaction to the bee sting.
Spring is the worst season for *allergic* asthma.

senses.gloss: Humorous: strongly disliking something.
examples: My brother is *allergic* to hard work.
She's *allergic* to meetings that could have been emails.

position: both — mostly after a verb (*He's addicted to heroin*); before a noun less often (*addicted gamblers*)
takes: *to* + noun or *-ing* (*addicted to heroin*, *addicted to playing video games*)
contrast: The *to* is a preposition, so a verb after it takes *-ing*: *addicted to gambling*, never ✗ *addicted to gamble*. Russian *зависимость от* pulls toward ✗ *addicted from*; English says *to*. *Addicted* describes the person; *addictive* describes the thing that causes it (*an addictive game*). *An addict* is the noun for the person, stressed AD-ikt.

senses.gloss: Physically and mentally unable to stop taking a drug or doing something harmful.
examples: He was *addicted* to painkillers for years.
Millions of Americans are *addicted* to nicotine.
She became *more addicted* to gambling after she lost her job.

senses.gloss: Informal: liking something so much that you do it all the time.
examples: I'm totally *addicted* to this show.
The kids are *addicted* to their phones.

position: both — *a loyal friend*, *She's loyal to the company*
takes: *to* + person, group or cause (*loyal to her friends*)
contrast: *Loyal to*, never ✗ *loyal with* or ✗ *loyal for*. False friend: Russian *лояльный* often means tolerant or lenient (*лояльный начальник* is *a lenient boss*, *лояльно относиться* is *be tolerant of*). English *loyal* means only faithful and devoted. *Loyal customers* keep buying from the same company; *a loyalty program* rewards them.

senses.gloss: Always supporting a person, group or country and not turning against them.
examples: He's been a *loyal* friend for thirty years.
The senator stayed *loyal* to the party.
Dogs are *more loyal* than cats, or so people say.

senses.gloss: Of customers or fans: continuing to buy from or support the same business or team.
examples: The diner has a small but *loyal* group of regulars.
Cubs fans are some of the *most loyal* in baseball.

position: both — *superior quality*, *This model is superior*
comparison: not gradable — it already compares: *far superior*, *vastly superior*, never *more superior*; the *arrogant* sense can take *more*
takes: *to* + noun (*superior to the old model*)
contrast: *Superior to*, never ✗ *superior than*: the word comes from Latin and already means 'higher', so it takes *to*, like *prefer to*. For the same reason avoid ✗ *more superior*; say *far superior* or *much superior*. *A superior* is also a noun (a boss or officer: *my superior*). *Superior* in anatomy means 'higher up in the body' (*the superior vena cava*). Russian *превосходный* (excellent) is often *excellent*; *superior* in ads is a selling word.

senses.gloss: Better than someone or something else.
examples: The new phone is *superior* to the old one in every way.
Their team was far *superior*.
Many chefs believe cast iron is *superior* for searing meat.

senses.gloss: Of very high quality.
examples: The hotel offers *superior* service at a fair price.
We only use *superior* ingredients.

senses.gloss: Behaving as if you are better than other people.
examples: She gave me a *superior* smile.
He always sounds so *superior* when he talks about his school.

senses.gloss: Higher in rank or position.
examples: He refused an order from a *superior* officer.
Soldiers must salute *superior* officers.

senses.gloss: Greater in number or strength.
examples: The army retreated in the face of *superior* numbers.
The enemy had *superior* weapons.

position: both — *inferior goods*, *This one is inferior*
comparison: not gradable — it already compares: *far inferior*, *vastly inferior*, never *more inferior*
takes: *to* + noun (*inferior to the original*)
contrast: *Inferior to*, never ✗ *inferior than*, and not ✗ *more inferior*: use *far inferior* or *much inferior*. *Feel inferior* is to feel less good or less important than others; the noun is *an inferiority complex* (комплекс неполноценности). *Inferior* is stronger and more formal than *worse*: in speech Americans often say *not as good as*.

senses.gloss: Not as good as someone or something else; of low quality.
examples: The sequel was far *inferior* to the original movie.
Cheap tools are often made from *inferior* steel.
Their product is *inferior* in almost every way.

senses.gloss: Of a person: feeling less important, clever or skilled than others.
examples: Her rich friends always made her feel *inferior*.
Nobody should be treated as *inferior* because of where they come from.

senses.gloss: Lower in rank or position.
examples: He never accepted an *inferior* role on the team.
In the old army, sergeants were *inferior* in rank to lieutenants.

position: both — *eligible voters*, *You're eligible for a refund*
comparison: not gradable — in the *allowed by the rules* sense; *most eligible* only in the *marriage* sense
takes: *for* + noun (*eligible for a scholarship*); *to*-infinitive (*eligible to vote*)
contrast: *Eligible for* + noun, *eligible to* + verb: *eligible for a discount*, *eligible to apply*. Never ✗ *eligible on* or ✗ *eligible to a discount*. *Eligible* is about meeting rules and conditions (*имеющий право*, *соответствующий требованиям*), not about ability. Don't confuse it with *legible* (разборчивый, about handwriting). *An eligible bachelor* is an attractive man to marry, often *the most eligible bachelor in town*.

senses.gloss: Allowed by the rules to do or get something because you meet the conditions.
examples: You're *eligible* for a refund within 30 days.
At 18, she'll be *eligible* to vote.
Only full-time employees are *eligible* for the bonus.

senses.gloss: Of an unmarried person: attractive as a husband or wife, often because of money or status.
examples: He was the *most eligible* bachelor in Dallas.
Her mother kept introducing her to *eligible* young men.

position: both — *a qualified nurse*, *She's qualified for the job*
takes: *for* + job or position (*qualified for the job*); *to*-infinitive (*qualified to teach*); *as* + role (*qualified as a pilot*); *in* + field (*qualified in nursing*)
contrast: *Qualified for* a job, *qualified to* do something, *qualified as* a role: *She's qualified for the position*, *He's not qualified to give legal advice*, *qualified as an electrician*. *I'm not qualified to say* is a modest way to say you don't know enough. *A qualified success* or *qualified support* is only partial, with conditions — the opposite of what learners expect. Russian *квалифицированный рабочий* is usually *a skilled worker*.

senses.gloss: Having the training, experience or certificates needed for a job or activity.
examples: We need a *qualified* electrician to do the wiring.
She's the *most qualified* candidate for the job.
He's *qualified* as a nurse but works in sales.

senses.gloss: Having the knowledge or right to do or judge something.
examples: I'm not really *qualified* to comment on that.
Only a doctor is *qualified* to make that decision.

senses.gloss: Limited or not complete; with conditions.
examples: The launch was only a *qualified* success.
The committee gave the plan its *qualified* approval.

position: both — after a verb (*Students are exempt*); before a noun (*exempt employees*)
takes: *from* + noun or *-ing* (*exempt from taxes*, *exempt from paying*)
contrast: *Exempt from*, never ✗ *exempt of*: Russian *освобождён от* matches *from*. *Exempt* is also a verb with the same form (*The law exempts small businesses from the tax*). In American workplaces, *exempt* employees are salaried and not paid overtime; *non-exempt* employees are paid by the hour and get overtime. *Tax-exempt* is a compound: *a tax-exempt charity*.

senses.gloss: Not required to do or pay something that others must.
examples: Churches are *exempt* from property taxes.
Seniors are *exempt* from taking the test.
Medical supplies were *exempt* from the new tariffs.

senses.gloss: In US employment: paid a salary and not entitled to overtime pay.
senses.ru: (о сотруднике) на окладе, без оплаты сверхурочных
examples: Managers are *exempt* employees, so they don't get overtime.
The job is classified as *exempt*.

position: both — *a safe place*, *You're safe now*
takes: *from* + danger (*safe from attack*); *for* + person (*safe for kids*); *with* + person (*The secret is safe with me*); *to*-infinitive (*safe to drink*)
contrast: *Safe from* is protected against a danger (*safe from the storm*); *safe for* is not harmful to someone (*safe for pets*). Russian *безопасный* (not dangerous) and *в безопасности* (not in danger) are both *safe* in English: *a safe city* and *We're safe here*. *Safe* is also a noun: *a safe* (сейф). *Drive safe* is common American speech, but careful English uses the adverb: *drive safely*. *Secure* is close but more about being protected by locks, guards or systems.

senses.gloss: Not in danger; protected from harm.
examples: The kids are *safe* at home with their grandparents.
After the storm, everyone was *safe* and sound.
We'll be *safe* from the rain under the bridge.

senses.gloss: Not likely to cause harm or danger.
examples: Is the water *safe* to drink?
This is one of the *safest* neighborhoods in the city.
These toys aren't *safe* for children under three.

senses.gloss: Not involving risk; cautious.
examples: It's a *safe* bet that prices will go up again.
Take an umbrella, just to be on the *safe* side.
He's a very *safe* driver.

senses.gloss: Kept where it will not be lost, damaged or stolen.
examples: Keep your passport in a *safe* place.
Don't worry — your secret is *safe* with me.

senses.gloss: In baseball: reaching a base without being put out.
examples: The umpire called him *safe* at second.
She slid into home and was *safe*.

position: both — *free tickets*, *Are you free tonight?*
takes: *of* + noun (without: *free of charge*, *free of pain*); *from* + noun (not controlled or affected by: *free from fear*); *to*-infinitive (*free to leave*); *for* + noun (not busy: *free for lunch*); *with* + noun (generous: *free with advice*)
contrast: One English word covers both *бесплатный* and *свободный*, so *free food* and *a free country* use the same word. *Free* alone or *for free* means costing nothing (*I got it for free* is informal; *free of charge* is formal); ✗ *for freely* is wrong. *Free of* and *free from* are close, but *free of* leans toward 'without' (*free of sugar*) and *free from* toward 'not suffering from' (*free from pain*, *free from fear*). The comparative *freer* has two *e*s and is said FREE-ur. In *Kids get in free*, *free* is an adverb; in *free the prisoners* it is a verb.

senses.gloss: Costing nothing.
examples: The museum is *free* on Sundays.
We got two *free* tickets to the game.
Delivery is *free* for orders over fifty dollars.

senses.gloss: Able to do, say or choose what you want; not controlled by others.
examples: You're *free* to leave at any time.
The press should be *free* to criticize the government.
As kids, we were much *freer* to roam the neighborhood.

senses.gloss: Not in prison or held by someone.
examples: After twenty years, he was finally a *free* man.
The hostages were set *free* on Tuesday.

senses.gloss: Not busy; having no plans at a certain time.
examples: Are you *free* for lunch tomorrow?
What do you do in your *free* time?

senses.gloss: Not being used or occupied.
examples: Excuse me, is this seat *free*?
Keep one hand *free* to hold the railing.

senses.gloss: Without something unpleasant or unwanted.
examples: She's been *free* of cancer for five years.
The roads should be *free* from ice by noon.

senses.gloss: Not fixed or held in place.
examples: Tie the *free* end of the rope to the tree.
He pulled his arm *free* and ran.

senses.gloss: Giving or using something generously, sometimes too much.
examples: My uncle is very *free* with his advice.
She's always been *free* with her money.

senses.gloss: Of a translation: not following the original word for word.
examples: It's a *free* translation, but it keeps the spirit of the poem.
The movie is a *free* adaptation of the novel.

position: both — *absent students*, *He was absent yesterday*
comparison: not gradable — in the *not there* sense
takes: *from* + place or event (*absent from school*, *absent from the meeting*)
contrast: *Absent from*, never ✗ *absent at*, ✗ *absent in* or ✗ *absent on*: *absent from class*. *Absent* is formal and used about school, work and official records; in speech Americans say *out* or *not here* (*She's out today*). The verb *absent yourself* is stressed ab-SENT and is very formal. In formal American English *absent* is also used as a preposition meaning 'without' (*Absent new evidence, the case is closed*), which is not the adjective. *Absent-minded* (рассеянный) is a compound.

senses.gloss: Not in a place where you are expected to be, such as school or work.
examples: Three students were *absent* from class today.
He was *absent* from work for a week with the flu.
The mayor was noticeably *absent* from the ceremony.

senses.gloss: Not existing or not present in something.
examples: Humor is completely *absent* from his books.
The symptoms are often *absent* in young patients.

senses.gloss: Of a look or manner: showing that you are thinking about something else.
examples: She nodded with an *absent* smile.
He had an *absent* look in his eyes.

position: both — *a curious child*, *I'm curious about it*
takes: *about* + noun (*curious about her past*); *to*-infinitive (*curious to see*); *wh*-clause (*curious why he left*)
contrast: *Curious about*, never ✗ *curious in* or ✗ *curious of*: *I'm curious about the new job*. English *curious* is positive or neutral (wanting to learn); Russian *любопытный* can also mean nosy, which is *nosy* in English (*a nosy neighbor*). *I'm curious* is also a polite way to ask a question: *Just curious — where did you buy that?* *Curious* meaning 'strange' is a little formal; in speech *weird* or *strange* is more common.

senses.gloss: Wanting to know or learn about something.
examples: Kids are naturally *curious* about everything.
I'm *curious* to see how the movie ends.
The more she read, the *more curious* she got.

senses.gloss: Strange and unusual.
examples: A *curious* thing happened on the way home.
It's *curious* that nobody noticed the door was open.

position: both — *a serious problem*, *Are you serious?*
takes: *about* + noun or *-ing* (*serious about her career*, *serious about quitting*)
contrast: *Serious about*, never ✗ *serious in* or ✗ *serious to*: *He's serious about getting in shape*. *Are you serious?* can express surprise or disbelief (*ты серьёзно?*), just like *Seriously?*. For illness and injury, English uses *serious*, not *heavy*: *a serious injury* (тяжёлая травма), *seriously ill*. *A serious relationship* is a long-term one. In informal American English *serious money* means a lot of money.

senses.gloss: Bad or dangerous enough to worry about.
examples: He was taken to the hospital with *serious* injuries.
Climate change is a *serious* problem.
The damage was *more serious* than we thought.

senses.gloss: Meaning what you say; not joking.
examples: Are you *serious*? You quit your job?
I'm *serious* — I really saw a bear.

senses.gloss: Determined and really intending to do something or stay with someone.
examples: If you're *serious* about losing weight, cut out soda.
They've been dating for a year, and it's getting *serious*.
Is she in a *serious* relationship?

senses.gloss: Of a person: quiet, thoughtful and not often laughing.
examples: She was a *serious* child who loved books.
Why do you look so *serious*?

senses.gloss: Needing careful thought; important rather than for fun.
examples: The proposal deserves *serious* consideration.
He reads *serious* literature, not thrillers.

senses.gloss: Informal: large or impressive in amount or quality.
examples: That house must have cost some *serious* money.
These guys are *serious* cooks.

position: both — *a careful driver*, *Be careful!*
takes: *with* + thing you handle (*careful with that knife*, *careful with money*); *about* + noun or *-ing* (*careful about what you eat*); *of* + noun (*careful of the ice*); *to*-infinitive (*careful to lock the door*, *careful not to wake her*)
contrast: The preposition changes what you are careful about. *Careful with* is handling something (*careful with the glasses*); *careful about* is choosing or deciding (*careful about who you trust*); *careful of* is avoiding a danger (*careful of the step*). Use the adverb for how you do something: *Drive carefully*, not ✗ *Drive careful* in careful English. Russian *аккуратный* is often *neat* or *tidy* (*аккуратный почерк* is *neat handwriting*), not *careful*.

senses.gloss: Paying attention so that you avoid danger, mistakes or damage.
examples: Be *careful* — the floor is wet.
Please be *careful* with that vase.
I'll be *more careful* next time, I promise.

senses.gloss: Done with a lot of attention to detail.
examples: After *careful* thought, she turned down the offer.
The report is based on a *careful* study of the data.
The house needs *careful* cleaning before we sell it.

senses.gloss: careful with money: not spending more than you need to.
examples: My parents were always *careful* with money.
We have to be *careful* until I find a new job.

position: both — *a busy street*, *I'm busy*
takes: *with* + noun (*busy with work*); *-ing* directly, with no preposition (*busy cooking*); *at* + place or task (*busy at work*)
contrast: A verb after *busy* takes *-ing* with no preposition: *She's busy packing*, never ✗ *busy to pack* or ✗ *busy with packing*. Use *with* only before a noun: *busy with the kids*. Russian *занято* is not always *busy*: a seat is *taken*, a restroom is *occupied*, but a phone line in the US is *busy* (*I got a busy signal*). The noun *business* (бизнес, дело) comes from *busy* but is said BIZ-nuhs.

senses.gloss: Having a lot to do; working and not free.
examples: Sorry, I can't talk now — I'm *busy*.
She's *busy* getting the kids ready for school.
He's been *busy* with work all week.

senses.gloss: Of a time: full of activity.
examples: I've had a really *busy* day.
December is the *busiest* month of the year for stores.

senses.gloss: Of a place: full of people or traffic.
examples: They live on a *busy* street near downtown.
The airport is *busier* than usual this weekend.
The restaurant was too *busy* to get a table.

senses.gloss: Of a phone line: already being used, so you cannot get through.
examples: I called three times, but the line was *busy*.
All I get is a *busy* signal.

senses.gloss: Of a design or picture: having too many details or colors.
examples: The wallpaper is a little too *busy* for a small room.
The website looks cluttered and *busy*.

position: both — mostly after a verb (*We're delighted*); before a noun less often (*delighted fans*)
comparison: more/most — *more delighted*; usually strengthened with *absolutely* or *really*, not *very*
takes: *with* + thing or person (*delighted with the gift*); *at* or *by* + news or event (*delighted at the news*); *to*-infinitive (*delighted to meet you*); *that*-clause
contrast: *Delighted* is the feeling; *delightful* describes what causes it: *We were delighted with the hotel* but *The hotel was delightful*. *Delighted with* is common for a thing you have (*delighted with her new car*); *at* and *by* for news or an event (*delighted at the result*). *I'd be delighted* is a warm, polite yes to an invitation. Because *delighted* is already strong, *very delighted* sounds odd; say *absolutely delighted* or *really delighted*.

senses.gloss: Very pleased and happy.
examples: We're *delighted* with the new house.
She was *delighted* to hear that you're coming.
"Would you like to join us?" "I'd be *delighted*."

position: both — mostly after a verb (*He's obsessed with her*); before a noun less often (*an obsessed fan*)
takes: *with* + noun or *-ing* (*obsessed with her weight*, *obsessed with winning*); *by* + noun, more formal (*obsessed by fear*)
contrast: *Obsessed with*, not ✗ *obsessed on* or ✗ *obsessed about*: *She's obsessed with K-pop*. The verb takes *about* or *over*: *Stop obsessing about it*. *Obsessed* describes the person; *obsessive* describes behavior or a type of person (*obsessive cleaning*). In casual American speech *I'm obsessed with this!* is just strong liking, like *я подсела*, not a medical problem.

senses.gloss: Thinking about someone or something all the time, in a way that is not normal or healthy.
examples: He's *obsessed* with his ex-girlfriend.
She became *obsessed* with losing weight.
The more he lost, the *more obsessed* with gambling he got.

senses.gloss: Informal: liking something very much.
examples: I'm *obsessed* with this song right now.
My daughter is *obsessed* with horses.

position: both — *a patient teacher*, *Be patient*
takes: *with* + person or thing (*patient with the kids*)
contrast: *Patient with*, never ✗ *patient to* or ✗ *patient for*: *She's patient with her students*. The same spelling is also the noun *a patient* (пациент), which learners know first. *Patience* (терпение) and *patients* (пациенты) sound the same: *The doctor has patience with her patients*.

senses.gloss: Able to wait, or to deal with problems or difficult people, without getting angry.
examples: Be *patient* — the bus will be here soon.
She's very *patient* with young children.
I need to be *more patient* with my mom.

senses.gloss: Done carefully over a long time.
examples: The discovery came after years of *patient* research.
With *patient* work, they restored the old house.

position: both — *a skilled surgeon*, *She's skilled at negotiating*
takes: *at* + noun or *-ing* (*skilled at chess*, *skilled at fixing things*); *in* + field or *-ing* (*skilled in carpentry*)
contrast: *Skilled at* and *skilled in* are both correct; *in* is more common with a field (*skilled in accounting*), *at* with an activity (*skilled at getting deals*). Never ✗ *skilled on*. *Skilled* describes the person or the work; *skillful* describes how something is done (*a skillful performance*). American spelling is *skillful*, British *skilful*. *Skilled labor* and *skilled workers* mean workers with training, Russian *квалифицированные рабочие*.

senses.gloss: Having the ability and experience to do something well.
examples: She's a highly *skilled* surgeon.
He's very *skilled* at calming angry customers.
The younger players are *more skilled* than we were.

senses.gloss: Of work or workers: needing or having special training.
examples: There's a shortage of *skilled* workers in the region.
Welding is *skilled* work that pays well.

position: both — *a hopeless situation*, *I'm hopeless at math*
takes: *at* + noun or *-ing* (very bad at: *hopeless at math*); *with* + thing (*hopeless with money*)
contrast: *Hopeless at* is being very bad at a skill (*hopeless at cooking*); *hopeless with* is bad at handling something (*hopeless with names*). Don't confuse *hopeless* (безнадёжный) with *helpless* (беспомощный). *A hopeless romantic* is someone who will always be romantic, with no hope of changing — a friendly, joking phrase.

senses.gloss: With no chance of success or improvement.
examples: The situation looked *hopeless*.
It's *hopeless* — we'll never find the keys in all this snow.
Things seemed *more hopeless* every day.

senses.gloss: Very bad at doing something — informal.
examples: I'm *hopeless* at math.
He's *hopeless* with names.
She's a *hopeless* cook.

senses.gloss: Feeling that nothing good will happen.
examples: After months without work, he felt *hopeless*.
She gave me a *hopeless* look.

senses.gloss: Before a noun: complete, and not able to change.
examples: I'm a *hopeless* romantic.
He's a *hopeless* optimist.

position: both — *an experienced driver*, *She's very experienced*
takes: *in* + field or *-ing* (*experienced in sales*); *at* + *-ing* (*experienced at handling complaints*); *with* + tools, people or situations (*experienced with kids*)
contrast: *Experienced in* a field, *at* an activity, *with* a tool or group: *experienced in marketing*, *experienced at negotiating*, *experienced with children*. Never ✗ *experienced on*. Russian *опытный* has a second meaning, *experimental*: *опытный образец* is *a prototype*, *опытное поле* is *an experimental field*, never ✗ *an experienced field*. The noun *experience* is both *опыт* (knowledge) and *впечатление* (an event).

senses.gloss: Having knowledge or skill from doing something for a long time.
examples: We need an *experienced* nurse for the night shift.
She's very *experienced* in family law.
The *most experienced* players on the team help the rookies.

position: both — *a successful business*, *The operation was successful*
takes: *in* + noun or *-ing* (*successful in getting a loan*); *at* + noun or *-ing* (*successful at attracting customers*); *as* + role (*successful as a writer*)
contrast: A verb after *successful* takes *in* or *at* + *-ing*: *successful in finding a job*, never ✗ *successful to find*. The verb works the same way: *She succeeded in finding it*. Spelling: two *c*s, two *s*s, one *l*. Don't confuse it with *successive* (последовательный, one after another): *three successive wins*.

senses.gloss: Achieving what was intended.
examples: The surgery was completely *successful*.
Were you *successful* in getting a refund?
This year's fundraiser was *more successful* than last year's.

senses.gloss: Having achieved money, status or fame in your work.
examples: Her father is a *successful* lawyer in Boston.
He became very *successful* as a songwriter.

senses.gloss: Of a business, product or work: popular and making money.
examples: They own a *successful* chain of restaurants.
It was the *most successful* movie of the year.

position: predicative only — *Support was lacking*, *He's lacking in confidence*
comparison: not gradable — degree comes from adverbs: *sadly lacking*, *seriously lacking*
takes: *in* + quality (*lacking in confidence*, *lacking in experience*)
contrast: Three patterns, and learners mix them. The adjective takes *in*: *He's lacking in experience*. The verb takes a direct object with no preposition: *He lacks experience*, never ✗ *He lacks of experience*. The noun takes *of*: *a lack of experience*. Russian *не хватает* is usually the verb or noun in everyday English: *We don't have enough time* or *There's a lack of time*. *Lacking* alone after a verb means 'missing' or 'not good enough': *Evidence is lacking*.

senses.gloss: Not there, or not available in the amount needed; not good enough.
examples: Real leadership has been *lacking* in this company for years.
Evidence against him is *lacking*.
I found the service sadly *lacking*.

senses.gloss: lacking in: not having enough of a quality.
examples: The food was *lacking* in flavor.
She's smart but *lacking* in experience.

position: both — mostly after a verb (*She was absorbed in her book*); before a noun less often (*an absorbed expression*)
takes: *in* + activity or thought (*absorbed in a book*, *absorbed in thought*)
contrast: *Absorbed in*, not ✗ *absorbed with* or ✗ *absorbed by*: *He was absorbed in his work* (был поглощён работой). *Absorbed by* is a passive verb about liquid, heat or companies, not this adjective: *The water was absorbed by the towel*; *The company was absorbed by a bigger one*. *Absorbing* describes what holds your attention (*an absorbing novel*). *Self-absorbed* is a compound meaning only interested in yourself.

senses.gloss: Giving all your attention to something, so that you do not notice anything else.
examples: She was so *absorbed* in her book that she missed her stop.
He sat there, *absorbed* in thought.
The kids became *more absorbed* in the game with every level.

position: both — *an intent look*, *She's intent on winning*
takes: *on* or formal *upon* + noun or *-ing* (*intent on revenge*, *intent on winning*)
contrast: *Intent on* + *-ing*, never ✗ *intent to win* as an adjective. The noun *intent* is different and does take *to*: *with intent to kill* (с умыслом убить), *a letter of intent*. In everyday English the noun is usually *intention* (*I have no intention of leaving*). Don't confuse *intent* with *intense* (сильный, напряжённый). *Intent* stresses the second syllable: in-TENT.

senses.gloss: Determined to do something, often in spite of problems.
examples: He seems *intent* on ruining the party.
The team is *intent* on winning the title this year.
She was *more intent* than ever on finishing school.

senses.gloss: Giving all your attention to something.
examples: She had an *intent* look on her face as she read the letter.
The boys were *intent* on their video game.

position: both — *a torn shirt*, *I'm torn*
comparison: not gradable — degree comes from adverbs: *badly torn*, *really torn*
takes: *between* + two choices (*torn between two jobs*); *about* or *over* + decision (*torn about moving*)
contrast: *Torn between* two choices, never ✗ *torn among* two or ✗ *torn from* two: *I'm torn between the red one and the blue one* (не могу выбрать между). *Torn* alone after *be* also means you can't decide: *I'm really torn*. The verb is *tear* (/tɛr/, rip), *tore*, *torn*; don't confuse it with *tear* (/tɪr/, a drop from the eye). *War-torn* is a compound: *a war-torn country* (раздираемая войной страна).

senses.gloss: Ripped or damaged by being pulled apart.
examples: He showed up in *torn* jeans and a T-shirt.
The quarterback is out for the season with a *torn* ligament.
The pages of the old book were *torn* and yellow.

senses.gloss: Unable to decide between two things you want or feel.
examples: I'm *torn* between taking the job and staying here.
She was *torn* about whether to tell him.
Many voters feel *torn* over the issue.

position: both — *a divided country*, *Opinion is divided*
takes: *on* or *over* + issue (*divided on abortion*, *divided over the plan*); *about* + issue; *between* + groups or places (*her time is divided between two offices*)
contrast: For opinions, use *divided on* or *divided over*: *The town is divided over the new school* (город расколот из-за). *Divided into* parts is usually a passive verb, not this adjective: *The book is divided into three chapters*. *Divided by* in math is also a verb: *Ten divided by two is five*. *A divided highway* in the US is a road with a strip between the two directions.

senses.gloss: Of a group: disagreeing strongly, so that it is split into sides.
examples: The country has never been *more divided*.
Experts are *divided* on whether the drug works.
The family was *divided* over what to do with the farm.

senses.gloss: Split into separate parts, or between two places or loyalties.
examples: Take the *divided* highway north for ten miles.
He has *divided* loyalties, with friends on both teams.
Her time is *divided* between New York and Miami.

position: both — *a worthy cause*, *She's worthy of the award*
takes: *of* + noun or *-ing* (*worthy of respect*, *worthy of being remembered*); *to*-infinitive, formal (*worthy to lead*)
contrast: *Worthy* needs *of* before a noun: *worthy of attention*, never ✗ *worthy attention*. *Worth* works the other way and takes no preposition: *worth ten dollars*, *worth seeing*, never ✗ *worth of seeing*. So: *The book is worth reading* but *The book is worthy of attention*. *Worthy* often sounds formal; in speech Americans say *deserve*: *She deserves the award*. *A worthy cause* is a charity or goal that deserves support.

senses.gloss: Deserving respect, attention or a particular reward.
examples: His idea is *worthy* of serious consideration.
There's no *worthier* candidate for the job.
I don't feel *worthy* of all this praise.

senses.gloss: Good and deserving support or respect.
examples: All the money goes to a *worthy* cause.
They were *worthy* opponents, and we were lucky to win.

position: both — *an envious look*, *She's envious of her sister*
takes: *of* + person or thing (*envious of his success*)
contrast: Russian *завидовать кому-то* uses the dative, but English needs *of*: *envious of her*, never ✗ *envious to her*. The verb *envy* takes a direct object with no preposition: *I envy you*. *Envious* means only wanting what someone else has; *jealous* can mean that too, but also fear of losing a partner (*ревность*). *Enviable* describes the thing that others envy (*an enviable lifestyle*).

senses.gloss: Wanting something that someone else has.
examples: Her friends were *envious* of her new job in Paris.
He gave the sports car an *envious* look.
I've never been *more envious* of anyone in my life.

position: both — *a scared little boy*, *I'm scared*
takes: *of* + noun or *-ing* (*scared of spiders*, *scared of falling*); *to*-infinitive (*scared to jump*); *that*-clause (*scared that he'd leave*); *for* + person (*scared for her*)
contrast: *Scared* is the feeling; *scary* describes what causes it: *I was scared* but *The movie was scary*, never ✗ *I was scary* when you mean fear. *Scared of*, never ✗ *scared from* or ✗ *scared before*: Russian *бояться* + genitive becomes *of*.
